rating.reasoning_summary: This strand represents a recurring social ritual of book recommendation requests rather than an evolving narrative. Anchored by RichDecibels' 2021 'cognitive upgrade' tweet, it spawns annual variations (Tasshin's yearly 'five books' prompts) but the core mechanic remains static: 'Tell me what to read.' While it succeeds as network maintenance—revealing taste clusters and intellectual aspirations—there is no conceptual evolution. The 2024 innovation of 'The Reading Hour' (synchronous reading sessions) represents the only structural mutation, moving from asynchronous recommendation-gathering to coordinated practice. However, this remains a social technology for execution rather than knowledge production about reading itself.

essential_tweets.annotation: The Archetypal Prompt: Rich's original 'cognitive upgrade summer' tweet that establishes the aspirational frame
The Annual Ritual Begins: Tasshin transforms the prompt into a yearly practice with the 'five books by end of 2022' format
Meta-Commentary: Introduction of 'How to Talk About Books You Haven't Read,' revealing self-awareness about performative reading
Persistence Check: One year later, following up on whether people actually read their aspirational lists
The Meme Spreads: Tasshin adopts Rich's exact phrasing, showing the prompt's memetic stickiness
2023 Iteration: The ritual recurs, now with established format and expectations
Structural Innovation: Launch of 'The Reading Hour'—moving from recommendation lists to coordinated reading practice
Execution Details: The mechanics of synchronous silent reading sessions, quoting the original Rich tweet
Canonization: Tasshin curates a meta-thread about reading, positioning Rich's tweet as foundational text
The Eternal Return: Years later, the same desire ('I need to read more books') continues without resolution

title: “Cognitive upgrade” became Book Twitter’s yearly ritual
summary:
RichDecibels accidentally minted a meme in 2021 with: “It might be one of those summers where I read 10 or 20 books and have a cognitive upgrade,” i.e. a socially acceptable way to beg for recommendations while sounding like you’re leveling up your brain. People immediately played along (e.g. the_wilderless drops Mary Midgley’s *The Myths We Live By*), and Rich even came back a few days later with a pure addict’s “More please.”

Then tasshinfogleman turned the one-off thirst trap into an annual ceremony: “list five books you haven’t read yet…by the end of 2022/2023 so as to give yourself a cognitive upgrade,” directly quoting Rich like it’s scripture. The funniest peak is the self-awareness: dschorno tells everyone replying they need Pierre Bayard’s *How to Talk About Books You Haven’t Read*, and Tasshin replies with notes “in case you don’t want to read it but want to be able to talk about it,” including the perfect line: “I highly recommend not reading… I do suggest talking about it.” A year later Tasshin does the accountability lap—“did any of you read these books?”—and the replies are basically “uh… some chapters,” with uberstuber as the rare overachiever (“I read all of these except *Beginning of Infinity*”).

What dies every cycle is the idea that the list itself solves anything: it’s mostly status-flavored intention-setting, not a new theory of reading. The one real mutation arrives in 2024, when Tasshin launches “The Reading Hour,” a Zoom where everyone reads silently for ~55 minutes—switching the social tech from collecting aspirational lists to actually executing. If you care about why smart people keep failing the same “I’m going to read more” goal, this thread is the whole loop in miniature: vibe → list → performative meta-joke → soft accountability → repeat… unless you change the structure so the reading actually happens.
